client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I keep trying to focus at work, but these memories of her just come out of nowhere and I completely lose track of what I'm doing. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly — it feels like nothing can really change the fact that she's gone.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy weight right now, and those unexpected waves of memory are such a natural part of grieving someone you loved — your heart is simply reminding you how much she mattered. You're absolutely right that nothing can change the fact that she's gone, and I want you to know I'm not here to try to "fix" that loss or make it disappear. I'm curious, though — when those memories surface at work, what kinds of thoughts tend to follow them, and how do you usually respond to yourself in those moments?

client: Honestly, when a memory hits, my first thought is usually something like "you should have called her more" or "why didn't you visit that last time you had the chance." Then I just feel this wave of guilt on top of the sadness, and I end up telling myself to just push it down and get back to work, which doesn't really work. I guess I respond to myself pretty harshly — like I don't deserve to just sit with the memory, I have to punish myself for it too.
therapist: That self-awareness you just showed is really meaningful — you can see that you're not just grieving her, you're also being quite hard on yourself on top of the grief, almost like adding a second layer of pain. Those thoughts like "I should have called more" feel very convincing in the moment, but I'd gently invite you to consider: if a close friend came to you with those same regrets, would you tell them they deserved to be punished for being an imperfect human being? What do you think it would feel like to let yourself simply *have* the memory, without the verdict attached to it?

client: I hear what you're saying, and no, I wouldn't tell a friend they deserved to feel that way — that part makes sense in theory. But when it's me, it just feels different, like the guilt is actually telling me something true about how I failed her, not just a thought I can choose to set aside. I'm not sure I know how to just "have" a memory without my brain immediately going to what I did wrong.
therapist: That distinction you're making is so important — it *does* feel different when it's you, and that feeling of "this guilt must be true because it feels so real and heavy" is actually one of the most common and painful tricks our minds play on us during grief. The intensity of a feeling can make it seem like evidence, but guilt this strong often says more about how deeply you loved her than it does about any failure on your part. I'm wondering — when you think back on your relationship with her as a whole, what do you think *she* would say about the kind of person you were to her?

client: That question actually kind of stopped me for a second, because I think she would have said I was a good grandchild — she used to tell me that pretty regularly, actually. But then my brain immediately goes to "well, she was just being kind, she didn't know about all the times I let her down." I can see that I'm kind of arguing against any evidence that might make me feel less guilty, which is strange when I actually notice it like that.
therapist: That moment of noticing — "I'm arguing against the evidence" — is actually a really significant insight, because you just caught your mind doing something very specific: dismissing anything that challenges the guilt while accepting anything that supports it, which keeps the verdict locked in place no matter what. It's not strange at all that your brain does this; it's a very human way of holding onto a connection with someone we've lost, even if that connection feels painful. I'm curious — what might it mean about you, and about your love for her, if you allowed her words about you to be just as true as your harshest self-criticisms?

client: I guess if I let her words be just as true, it would mean that maybe I actually did love her well enough, at least most of the time — and that feels both comforting and terrifying at the same time, honestly. Comforting because it would mean I'm not the failure I keep telling myself I am, but terrifying because it feels like if I let go of the guilt, I'm somehow letting go of her too. Like the guilt is the last thing keeping me connected to her, which sounds kind of messed up when I say it out loud.
therapist: It doesn't sound messed up at all — it sounds like something really profound and true that you just uncovered about yourself, and that kind of insight can take people a long time to reach. Grief can make guilt feel like a form of loyalty, as if staying in pain is how we prove the relationship mattered, but I wonder if the love itself — the memories, the ways she shaped you, the fact that you're sitting here caring this deeply — might actually be a far more enduring connection to her than the guilt ever could be. What do you think she would want to be the thing that keeps her present in your life?

client: She would have wanted me to remember her through the good things — her cooking, her laugh, the way she always made me feel like I mattered just by walking in the door. That actually feels more right than anything I've said today, and I wasn't expecting this conversation to go here. I guess I'm just scared that if I try to shift toward that, the guilt is going to keep pulling me back and I won't be able to hold onto it.
therapist: What you just described — her cooking, her laugh, the way she made you feel — that *is* her, and that version of her sounds like someone who would absolutely be rooting for you to find your way back to those things. The guilt pulling you back is real, and I don't want to minimize that, but you've already shown today that you can notice the pull and gently question it rather than just being swept away by it — that's not a small thing. I'm wondering if we could think of this as a small experiment: the next time a memory of her surfaces, what might it look like to just let yourself stay with one of those good things for even a few moments, before your mind rushes to the verdict?

client: I want to try that, I really do, but I'm worried that at work especially, when a memory hits out of nowhere, I'm going to be too caught off guard to remember to do any of this — it's one thing to think about it calmly here and another thing entirely when it actually happens. It feels like the guilt reaction is so fast and automatic that the good memory barely gets a chance before it's already been swallowed up. Is there something that might make it easier to actually catch that moment in real life, not just in theory?
therapist: You're identifying something really important — the gap between insight in a calm moment and actually catching yourself in the middle of a fast, automatic reaction is one of the most real challenges in this kind of work, and it's wise that you're thinking about it now rather than just hoping it will happen. One small thing that can help bridge that gap is creating a kind of "anchor" in advance — something very brief and concrete, like a single image of her laugh or even just her name, that you intentionally pair with the thought "this is how I carry her," so that when a memory hits, you have something specific and practiced to reach for rather than trying to build the whole thing from scratch in a flooded moment. Would it feel manageable to think of just one image or memory of her — something small and warm — that could serve as that anchor, something we could name together right now so it's already waiting for you when you need it?

client: There's actually one thing that comes to mind immediately — she had this specific way of laughing where she'd cover her mouth with her hand, like she was trying to hold it in but couldn't, and it always made everyone around her laugh too. That image feels warm in a way that doesn't immediately drag me toward guilt, which is kind of surprising. I'm a little skeptical that just holding onto that image will be enough when I'm in the middle of a stressful workday, but I'm willing to try it and see what happens.
therapist: That image is absolutely beautiful, and the fact that it came to you immediately and feels warm tells me it's already alive in you in a way that belongs entirely to love, not loss. Your skepticism is completely fair — one image isn't a magic switch, and some days the guilt will still be loud, but the goal isn't perfection, it's just giving that warmth a fighting chance to show up alongside the pain rather than being crowded out entirely. So as a small experiment this week, I'm wondering if you'd be willing to notice what happens — not to judge it, just to observe — when you reach for her laugh in one of those caught-off-guard moments, and maybe even jot down briefly what you felt before and after?

client: Writing it down feels like it might actually make it more real and harder to ignore, which I think is both the point and also what makes me nervous about it. I'm worried that on a bad day, looking back at what I wrote could just reinforce how often I'm failing at this rather than helping. But I guess I can try to just treat it as information rather than a report card — I'm not totally sure I'll manage that, but it seems worth attempting.
therapist: The fact that you already reframed it yourself — "information rather than a report card" — shows that the same skill you're building around grief is starting to show up in how you're approaching this whole process, and that's really worth noticing. It's okay if some entries feel harder than others, because the point isn't to document success, it's just to get curious about what's actually happening inside you, the same way you got curious here today and ended up somewhere you weren't expecting. What would it feel like to write just one entry this week — even just a sentence or two — and see what it's actually like before deciding whether it's helping or hurting?

client: One sentence or two feels a lot more manageable than I was imagining — I think I was picturing having to write some big detailed account of everything I was feeling, which sounded exhausting. I can probably do that much, even on a hard day. I'm still not sure what I'll find when I actually try it, but I think I'm a little more open to finding out than I was when I walked in here today.
therapist: That shift from "I'm not sure talking will help" to "I'm a little more open to finding out" is not a small thing — you carried something really heavy into this conversation and you engaged with it honestly and bravely, and I think your grandmother's laugh would agree. One sentence, whenever a moment hits, just as information — and you've already got your anchor ready and waiting. What feels most important for you to hold onto from today as you head back into the week?
